deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.headline: How climate change fueled the deadly Southern California wildfires
deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.body: Climate change has likely contributed to the unprecedented wildfires that are raging through Southern California. Five wildfires -- the Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Woodley and Lidia fires -- were burning through Ventura and Los Angeles counties on Wednesday. At least five people have been killed and several others injured by the disaster, according to officials. While wildfires are a natural and necessary part of Earth's cycle, climate change and other more direct human influences have increased their likelihood. Climate change is making naturally occurring events more intense and more frequent, research shows. [source article excerpt omitted], a breakdown of the latest in climate science coming from 14 different federal agencies, published in November 2023. [source article excerpt omitted] Warming temperatures, drier conditions and shifts in precipitation are contributing to an increase in the frequency of large wildfires and acres of land burned in the U.S. each year, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The U.S. wildfire season has grown longer and shifted earlier in recent decades due to warmer springs, longer summer dry seasons and drier vegetation, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. About 85% of wildfires are started by humans, according to data from the U.S. Forest Service. Most are accidental, like an unattended campfire or sparks from a powerline. But this has been exacerbated by rapid urbanization in recent decades as humans continue building into nature, including areas that have historically experienced frequent natural wildfire activity, the data showed. More frequent, intense and variable extreme weather events, known as compound events, are another factor currently fueling wildfires in parts of the West -- like California. In recent years, parts of the state went from experiencing a major drought to an extended period of above average precipitation that allowed for abundant vegetation growth. A stretch of intense, record-breaking heat then followed, drying out much of this vegetation providing ample fuel for large and fast-growing wildfires. Larger, more intense and more destructive wildfires are worsening air quality in many regions of the contiguous U.S. and Alaska, according to the federal government's Fifth National Climate Assessment. But climate change was the primary factor that led to the severity of the wildfires. A perfect storm of weather and climate conditions, such as Santa Ana wind gusts up to 100 mph and low humidity, allowed for the rapid spread of the flames.

deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.headline: EPA staff face gag orders as hundreds of environmental grants terminated
deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.body: Environmental Protection Agency staff across the country have been barred from communicating with grantee partners they are supposed to oversee, multiple sources said. Many nonprofit groups have been frozen out of federal payment systems without notice. Melissa Bosworth, who runs a small nonprofit in Denver administering an EPA grant for rural tribal and school projects, described a communication blackout that began days after President Trump’s inauguration. Then, at the end of February, she received formal notice that her grant had been terminated. The termination notice, reviewed by ABC News, cited programmatic inefficiencies and a lack of demonstrable outcomes, making no reference to diversity, equity and inclusion orders. “It was about helping fight disparities on behalf of small cities and rural schools,” Bosworth said. She and dozens of other nonprofit leaders from California to Tennessee reported intermittent loss of access to the payment system. In Philadelphia, EPA staff were told as recently as last week not to process new awards or communicate with recipients. When employees pressed regional bosses, they were told to comply to avoid jeopardizing their jobs. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency has promised transparency, but former EPA officials argue the gag order undermines oversight. Rebecca Kaduru, president of the Institute for Sustainable Communities, said she has lost payment access weekly and one of her two EPA grants was terminated. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced more than 400 contract terminations, saying the agency had saved over $2 billion. The agency did not detail which contracts were canceled, but environmental justice and community change grants were hit hard. Over 100 organizations received $1.6 billion in community change grants last year through the bipartisan Infrastructure Reduction Act of 2022. On Tuesday, Zeldin sent a memo eliminating all environmental justice offices. Many nonprofit leaders say savings are overstated and were not given a chance to explain their work.

deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.headline: EPA Proposes Repeal of Power Plant Emission Rules, Citing Economic Growth
deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.body: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, joined by Republican lawmakers, announced Wednesday the agency’s plan to repeal two major power plant emission regulations. At a press conference, Zeldin called it “a historic day” and said the actions aimed to “both protect the environment and grow the economy.” The first rule targeted would require existing coal-fired and new natural gas plants to cut 90% of their carbon pollution using technologies like carbon capture. The second would revise the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS), tightening the emissions standard for toxic metals by 70% and requiring a 67% reduction in the mercury emissions standard specifically from lignite coal-fired power plants. Zeldin said the EPA will determine if fossil fuel plants significantly contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and whether those emissions endanger public health—key steps for rolling back the rules under the Clean Air Act. Power plants are the largest industrial source of greenhouse gases, according to the EPA. The agency estimates the changes could save over a billion dollars a year and lower consumer electricity costs. Zeldin stressed that the repeal is a proposal, not final, and that public comment would be accepted. He added that “if finalized, no power plant will be allowed to emit more than they do today.” Former EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy called the rationale “absolutely illogical and indefensible,” calling it a political play that favors the fossil fuel industry. Environmental groups have promised legal challenges. The Sierra Club’s climate policy director said the rollback would mean more climate disasters and health emergencies. An EPA spokesperson stated that unlike regional pollutants, greenhouse gas emissions are global, so public health harms have not been accurately attributed to the U.S. power sector. The agency is moving forward with the proposal while facing strong opposition from scientists and advocates.

deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.headline: COP30 ends with deal, but falls short of fossil fuel phaseout roadmap
deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.body: It took an extra day, but delegates at COP30, the United Nations' climate conference, have reached a deal on a final agreement. The agreement, however, falls far short of the high expectations many delegates, environmental groups and non-governmental organizations had going into the annual conference in Belém, Brazil. Despite more than 80 countries calling for a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels worldwide, the primary cause of human-amplified climate change, that demand did not make it into the final text. Although the conference took place in what's called the "gateway to the Amazon," the COP30 agreement also doesn't include any significant new initiatives to stop deforestation and protect the Amazon rainforest, known as "the lungs of the planet." "The venue bursting into flames couldn't be a more apt metaphor for COP30's catastrophic failure to take concrete action to implement a funded and fair fossil fuel phaseout," Jean Su, energy justice director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement to ABC News, referencing a fire that broke out Thursday at the COP30 venue. She added that negotiations keep hitting a wall because wealthy nations fail to offer needed financial support. Appearing to acknowledge the disappointment, COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago said during his closing plenary remarks that he would use his authority as president to create two roadmaps himself—one on halting deforestation, another on transitioning away from fossil fuels. The House on Wednesday cleared a Republican health care package, 216-211, that does not extend the expiring Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. Four moderate Republicans who had earlier Wednesday bucked GOP leaders and signed a Democratic-backed discharge petition voted in favor of the package. Rep. Thomas Massie was the only Republican no vote.

The measure now goes to the Senate, where it's unlikely to pass, meaning Congress is set to leave for the holiday recess as millions of Americans will see their health care premiums remain largely stable.

'We have the smallest majority in U.S. history,' Johnson said, noting that razor-thin margins make all procedural tools fair game. He was spotted huddling with moderates on the floor, describing the talks as 'intense fellowship.'

The rebellion came after the House Rules Committee blocked amendments to extend the subsidies. Johnson has resisted allowing an up-or-down vote on the extension, which was a central issue in the record 43-day government shutdown this fall. The four Republicans—Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick, Mike Lawler, Rob Bresnahan, and Ryan Mackenzie—gave a discharge petition the 218 signatures needed to force a vote, though that vote isn't expected until January 2026 at the earliest.

Lawler said he doesn't endorse the Democrats' bill as written but that 'when leadership blocks action entirely, Congress has a responsibility to act.' Fitzpatrick urged leadership to 'let the House work its will.' Bresnahan said doing nothing was not an option, and the petition was 'the only option remaining.'

The Senate already rejected a clean three-year extension of the subsidies in a pair of dueling health care votes last week, though several Republican senators crossed the aisle to join all Democrats in supporting it.

The Senate will soon vote on an amendment forcing all states to require photo identification at the polls. “There are no good excuses” not to, said Sen. John Husted, R-Ohio.

Minnesota's shifting rules mirror a national debate: when, if ever, is it discriminatory to ban Native American mascots? The Trump administration has weighed in forcefully. The Native American Guardians Association, which filed the complaint that triggered the Massapequa probe, advocates for respectful use but opposes costumes and face paint. deepseek__deepseek-v4-pro/misinfoqa/rewr.body:
Federal health officials are investigating the University of Michigan Health system after a former employee claimed she was fired for seeking a religious exemption from providing gender-affirming care. The Department of Health and Human Services announced the probe in mid-June, citing federal conscience laws known as the Church Amendments. The move follows an April 2024 ruling by U.S. District Judge Jane Beckering that dismissed the employee’s lawsuit, a decision the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit upheld last month, ending the parallel civil case.

Legal experts say the investigation is a new use of the amendments, which traditionally allowed providers to refuse abortions or sterilizations. Elizabeth Sepper, a law professor at the University of Texas at Austin, said the text of the laws does not cover gender-affirming care, but the administration is stretching them to permit refusal of such treatment or to misgender patients.

The employee, Valerie Kloosterman, worked as a physician assistant and sued in 2022 after being fired in 2021. She alleged the health system forced her to use pronouns that contradicted her religious beliefs and to make referrals for transition-related procedures. The health system denied wrongdoing, stating it accommodated her discomfort but required nondiscriminatory treatment once care began. With the appeals court affirming the dismissal, HHS’s investigation is now the central legal front. The agency could theoretically withhold Medicare and Medicaid funding, though former Biden administration general counsel Sam Bagenstos called such a step highly unusual and likely illegal.

Religious liberty groups welcomed the investigation. Kayla Toney of First Liberty Institute said HHS is enforcing existing protections. But critics argue the probes are meant to chill gender-affirming care, sending a message that the administration will support employees who object to treating transgender patients even in states where such care is legal.
